topic.title: The auction is the show
topic.claim: The cricket auction gets more coverage than half the matches because selling the drama is easier than selling the sport.
topic.moment: You spend a full evening glued to men raising paddles, more hooked than you were during an actual league game.

turn.believed: The auction is just the boring admin before the real cricket.
turn.actually: It's engineered entertainment; the bidding wars, the shock buys and the price reveals are content in themselves.

topic.because: A season is long and matches can be dull, but money and suspense never are. Numbers on a screen pull eyeballs cheaply, all off-season.
topic.payoff: When the price tag draws a bigger crowd than the player, the product is the spectacle, not the sport.
topic.behaviour: Leagues turn player auctions into prime-time televised events with full analysis.
topic.mechanism: Money and suspense hold attention cheaply across the long off-season.
topic.group: cricket fans who follow the league year-round
topic.send_to: the friend who watches the auction live but skips half the matches
topic.why_now: Auction season pulls numbers bigger than many games.

score.why: People watch the auction more than the matches and never ask why; naming the spectacle as the real product is a decent one-level-deeper, if a lighter take.

cover.headline: The auction you call a formality is [what you actually watch]
cover.sub: Two hours of paddles. Then the season reached you as notifications.

paragraphs: The auction you call a formality is what you actually watch.
slides.why_swipe: A formality? I only check who my team picks.

paragraphs: It's a weekday evening in the off-season. You open the auction stream for ten minutes, just to see who your team picks. Boring paperwork, you tell yourself.
Two hours later, the purse-left graphic in the corner is the only number you care about. You're typing "WHAT" in the group chat over a bowler you'd never heard of.
slides.why_swipe: Fine, but the real season grips you even harder, right?

paragraphs: Then the season starts. By the third week, most games reach you as score notifications on your lock screen.
A chase that's settled by the 14th over doesn't even make you unlock the phone. You check the table on Sunday and call that following it.
slides.why_swipe: So why did paddles beat the actual cricket?

paragraphs: Here's the part that makes it cheap. The auction needs no pitch, no toss, no rain delay. Just a room, a screen and a number that keeps going up.
And every few minutes it ends the same way. The hammer, the price, the camera cutting to a team table clapping or groaning. **A channel gets a full prime-time evening out of months with no cricket.**
slides.why_swipe: So is all of it just a TV trick?

paragraphs: Some of it is the good kind of drama. A kid from a domestic side watches his price climb live, and his teammates pile on him on camera.
That clip will get more views than most of his overs that season.
slides.why_swipe: So what do you actually remember from all this?

paragraphs: A few weeks into the season, you can still rattle off the five costliest buys, down to the lakh.
Then someone at work asks about one innings any of them has played.

end.save: Come back to this the next time auction night eats your whole evening.
end.send: The friend who watches the auction live but skips half the matches.
end.promise: Why the things we watch work.

draft.caption: I gave a paddle going up more of my evening than three full matches, and I'll do it again next year
draft.alt_text: A carousel arguing that the cricket player auction, which fans call a formality, is the part they actually watch. It follows a fan who opens the auction stream for ten minutes and stays for two hours, reacting in the group chat, then follows the real season mostly through lock-screen score notifications. It explains that the auction needs no pitch, toss or weather, just a room, a screen and rising numbers, so a channel can fill prime time in the off-season. It admits some of the drama is genuinely good for young players, and ends with the fan able to list the five costliest buys but reaching for the phone when asked about one innings any of them played.
